name: Montgomery, Alabama
kicker: Capital of Alabama · First Confederate capital and civil rights landmark
briefing: Montgomery, on the Alabama River, has been Alabama’s capital since 1846. In 1861, the Confederacy was founded there, and Jefferson Davis took his oath as its president at the state capitol, so the city is nicknamed the “Cradle of the Confederacy.” Less than a century later, Rosa Parks’s arrest there sparked a 381-day bus boycott led by Martin Luther King Jr., and in 1965 voting-rights marchers from Selma ended their 54-mile walk at that same capitol.

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: This city was formed in 1819 when two towns on the Alabama River merged, and it was named for an Irish-born general who died leading an American attack on Quebec in 1775. In 1846, it replaced Tuscaloosa [“tusk-uh-LOO-suh”] as its state’s capital.
tossups.r: In 1861, it became the first capital of the Confederacy. For 10 points, name this capital of Alabama.

tossups.p: Jefferson Davis lived in this city in a house now known as the First White House of the Confederacy. On February 18, 1861, he took the oath of office as the Confederacy’s provisional president on the portico of its state capitol.
tossups.r: This city is nicknamed the “Cradle of the Confederacy.” For 10 points, name this capital of Alabama.

tossups.p: In April 1861, Confederate Secretary of War LeRoy Pope Walker telegraphed orders from this city telling P. G. T. Beauregard [“BOH-ruh-gard”] to demand the surrender of Fort Sumter. Delegates from seceded Southern states had met here two months earlier to form a new nation.
tossups.r: Jefferson Davis took his oath of office here. For 10 points, name this Alabama city, the first Confederate capital before Richmond.

tossups.p: On December 5, 1955, thousands of people packed into and around Holt Street Baptist Church in this city to hear a 26-year-old minister speak about a protest that had begun that morning. That minister, the pastor of this city’s Dexter Avenue Baptist Church, was chosen to lead the protest.
tossups.r: It was a bus boycott sparked by the arrest of Rosa Parks. For 10 points, name this capital of Alabama.

tossups.p: In May 1961, a mob attacked Freedom Riders, including John Lewis, when their bus arrived at this city’s Greyhound station, which now houses a museum about the rides. The next night, federal marshals protected a crowd meeting at Ralph Abernathy’s First Baptist Church here.
tossups.r: In 1955, Rosa Parks was arrested on a bus in this city. For 10 points, name this capital of Alabama.

tossups.p: Water flows across a round black granite table carved with the names of 41 people who died during the civil rights movement at a memorial in this city designed by Maya Lin. That memorial stands outside the offices of the Southern Poverty Law Center.
tossups.r: Martin Luther King Jr. led a bus boycott here in 1955 and 1956. For 10 points, name this capital of Alabama.

tossups.p: Hundreds of steel monuments, one for each U.S. county where racial terror lynchings were documented, fill the National Memorial for Peace and Justice, which opened in this city in 2018. Lawyer Bryan Stevenson’s Equal Justice Initiative also opened the Legacy Museum here.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Alabama city where Rosa Parks’s arrest started a famous bus boycott.

tossups.p: In his January 1963 inaugural address at the state capitol in this city, Governor George Wallace vowed to defend segregation. That capitol stands at the top of Dexter Avenue, a block from the church where Martin Luther King Jr. had been pastor.
tossups.r: In 1965, voting-rights marchers from Selma ended their 54-mile walk at that capitol. For 10 points, name this capital of Alabama.

tossups.p: On March 25, 1965, Martin Luther King Jr. asked “How long?” and answered “Not long” in a speech in front of this city’s capitol, saying that “the arc of the moral universe is long, but it bends toward justice.”
tossups.r: His listeners had just finished a march from Selma. For 10 points, name this capital of Alabama.

tossups.p: F. Scott Fitzgerald met his future wife, Zelda Sayre, the daughter of a judge, at a dance in this city while he was stationed at a nearby army camp in 1918. A house the couple rented here in the early 1930s is now a museum about them.
tossups.r: Zelda had been born here in 1900. For 10 points, name this capital of Alabama, where Rosa Parks was arrested in 1955.

tossups.p: The country singer Hank Williams is buried in this city, which has a museum devoted to his music, and the singer and pianist Nat King Cole was born here in 1919. The Alabama River flows past its downtown.
tossups.r: Martin Luther King Jr. was a pastor here when he led a bus boycott in 1955. For 10 points, name this capital of Alabama.

tossups.p: In 1910, the Wright brothers opened a civilian flying school in this city, on land that later became Maxwell Air Force Base. That base is home to the Air University, which trains Air Force officers.
tossups.r: This city on the Alabama River was the Confederacy’s first capital. For 10 points, name this capital of Alabama.

tossups.p: L. B. Sullivan, a city commissioner in charge of this city’s police, sued _The New York Times_ for libel over a 1960 advertisement supporting Martin Luther King Jr. The Supreme Court ruled against him in 1964, making it harder for public officials to win libel suits.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Alabama city where King had led a bus boycott in 1955 and 1956.

tossups.p: Jo Ann Robinson, an English professor at this city’s Alabama State College, used the school’s copying machine to print thousands of leaflets calling for a one-day protest. Her group, the Women’s Political Council, had complained to city leaders about segregated buses for years.
tossups.r: That protest grew into a 381-day bus boycott. For 10 points, name this capital of Alabama.

tossups.p: In March 1955, fifteen-year-old Claudette Colvin was arrested for refusing to give up her bus seat in this city. She later joined _Browder v. Gayle_, a lawsuit against bus segregation named partly for this city’s mayor, W. A. Gayle.
tossups.r: Nine months after Colvin’s arrest, Rosa Parks was arrested here too. For 10 points, name this capital of Alabama.

clues.t: The state capital of Alabama, on the Alabama River
Rosa Parks’s arrest here on December 1, 1955, sparked a 381-day bus boycott led by Martin Luther King Jr.
First capital of the Confederate States of America (1861), before the capital moved to Richmond, Virginia
The 1965 voting-rights march from Selma ended at its state capitol
Martin Luther King Jr. was pastor of its Dexter Avenue Baptist Church from 1954 to 1960
Jefferson Davis took the oath as the Confederacy’s provisional president on the portico of its capitol (February 18, 1861)
Nicknamed the “Cradle of the Confederacy” and the “Birthplace of the Civil Rights Movement”
_Browder v. Gayle_ (1956) struck down its segregated buses, and the Supreme Court upheld the ruling
King ended the march with his “How Long, Not Long” speech in front of the capitol (March 25, 1965): “the arc of the moral universe is long”
A mob attacked Freedom Riders, including John Lewis, at its Greyhound bus station in May 1961
Governor George Wallace vowed to defend segregation in his 1963 inaugural address at its capitol
Claudette Colvin, 15, was arrested on one of its buses in March 1955; Jo Ann Robinson’s Women’s Political Council printed the boycott leaflets
Named for an Irish-born Continental Army general who was killed attacking Quebec in 1775
Formed in 1819 when two towns on the Alabama River merged; replaced Tuscaloosa as the state capital in 1846
Jefferson Davis lived in the house now called the First White House of the Confederacy
Secretary of War LeRoy Pope Walker telegraphed orders from here to demand Fort Sumter’s surrender (April 1861)
On December 5, 1955, a packed mass meeting at Holt Street Baptist Church heard King and voted to keep the boycott going
Maya Lin’s Civil Rights Memorial (1989): water flows over a black granite table naming 41 people who died in the movement
Bryan Stevenson’s Equal Justice Initiative opened the National Memorial for Peace and Justice and the Legacy Museum here in 2018
City commissioner L. B. Sullivan’s libel suit led to _New York Times v. Sullivan_ (1964)
Hometown of Zelda Sayre, who met F. Scott Fitzgerald at a dance here in 1918; a house they rented is now a museum
Country singer Hank Williams is buried here, and Nat King Cole was born here (1919)
The Wright brothers opened a flying school here in 1910, on land that became Maxwell Air Force Base, home of the Air University
King’s house here was bombed in January 1956, and he urged an angry crowd to stay nonviolent

trap.title: Montgomery, Selma, or Birmingham?
trap.body: Three Alabama cities are famous civil rights answers. The 1965 voting-rights march began in Selma, where state troopers attacked marchers on “Bloody Sunday” at the Edmund Pettus Bridge, and it ended in Montgomery. Birmingham is where King wrote his “Letter from Birmingham Jail” in 1963 and where a bombing at the 16th Street Baptist Church killed four girls. Some questions also want the Montgomery Bus Boycott itself, not the city.
trap.fix: Montgomery clues: the state capital, the Confederacy’s first capital, Jefferson Davis’s oath, Rosa Parks, Dexter Avenue Baptist Church, and the end of the march. Selma clues: the Edmund Pettus Bridge and Bloody Sunday. Birmingham clues: Bull Connor, the Children’s Crusade, and the 16th Street Baptist Church. If the question says “this event” or “this protest,” answer “Montgomery Bus Boycott.”
trap.line: Real answer line: Montgomery, Alabama (do not accept “Alabama” or “Selma”)
